Triggers.value: Night-time or waking up in the dark
A specific texture associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers
I drift off into a world of my own
make sure never to be alone with another person

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
I feel like an object, not like a person
You can never know who will harm you

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Threat: missing/none selected despite multiple current-danger and exposure-related items
issues.explanation: The profile contains several items implying an active sense of present threat or exposure (e.g., 'World is Dangerous', 'Exposed to Others', concealment to avoid being noticed), yet the Threat component is entirely absent. For this trauma type, such items would usually cohere with at least some explicit threat content; the omission makes the cross-node picture clinically uneven.

'World is Dangerous' expresses a broad ongoing threat belief, but the formulation specifies no active links into or out of Threat and no Threat items are endorsed. This makes the appraisal sit awkwardly in the formulation because it functions more like a threat belief than an isolated negative self-appraisal.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
issues.explanation: 'Concealing Clothing ... to avoid being noticed' implies active management of current interpersonal threat/visibility. With Threat completely unrepresented and no Trigger→Threat or Maladaptive Strategies→Threat linkage in the formulation, this strategy lacks a clear matching symptom target in the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: The Threat node is not clinically coherent here. 'Flashbacks' and 'Physical Reactivity' are re-experiencing/arousal responses rather than threat appraisals, while the only genuine threat appraisal selected is 'Threat from Strangers.' That mixes different constructs within one node.

vignette: Ethan, a 25‑year‑old housekeeper, grew up in a cramped apartment where the walls were thin and the nights often dark and silent. In the fifth grade, the day his mother’s temper snapped into a physical outburst, he was forced into a small, dim closet to keep the violence from reaching him. The closet’s rough, splintered floor, the texture of its wood that still lingers in his memory, became a tactile reminder of that night. When he later works late cleaning a nearby daycare, the sight of the dim hallway lights and the faint echo of a child’s cry send a cold shock through him. Those nighttime darkness, the harsh texture, and the children's crying instantly ignite his triggers. The moment the lights flicker low, he stops sweeping, drops his mop, and retreats into an imagined world of distant beaches, a fantasy escape that allows him to distance himself from the present. The triggers also pull the memory of that closet and the slap in its splintered wood back into focus, making him feel as if the past is happening again. The memory, when it resurfaces, overwhelms him. It feels like a film that plays on a loop, complete with the sting of that splinter against his hand and the echo of his mother’s angry voice. The sensory reliving is so vivid that he cannot finish cleaning the room; he stops, breathless, and retreats to his car. Each time he drops a responsibility, the silence of his car gives his mind space to replay that night, and the more he avoids tasks, the more the memory gains dominance. This avoidance deepens his negative appraisals: he believes others could see the bruises on his arms just by looking at him, that he has been reduced to an object of pity, and that anyone could harm him at any moment. The feeling of being exposed, coupled with the physicality of the splintered floor, makes every dim hallway a potential stage where others might witness his past. His belief that others see what happened to him makes the darkness of any night feel like a public display of his trauma, and the more he stays alone, the more he feels judged and dehumanized. The sense of constant threat—flashbacks that snap him into the past, sudden physical reactions that flare up at the sound of a child’s cry, and an unshakable hypervigilance—feeds back into his avoidance, keeping him in a state of chronic alertness. At his job, when a new client asks him to clean after a night shift, he declines, fearing that the late hours will bring the same darkness and triggers. The fear of harm, the belief that his past makes him vulnerable, and the hypervigilant state that persists after each flashback drive him to keep workdays short and to avoid being the only person in the house when it gets dark. This avoidance has had concrete occupational consequences: a client’s request for him to stay past midnight was turned down, and the manager has begun to question his reliability. Ethan’s repeated dropping of responsibilities, fantasy escapes, and insistence on never being alone have left him isolated and anxious, reinforcing his feeling that he is exposed and that others view him as a fragile object. In the quiet hours after work, the rough texture of the car seat’s upholstery brings the closet memory rushing back, and he wakes up in the dark, drenched in sweat, certain that the threat is real. He finally turned to therapy after a week of sleepless nights, a missed appointment, and a deepening belief that he was losing control of his life. He fears that the hypervigilance will continue to erode his relationships and career, yet he hopes for a way to quiet the relentless memories and to feel safe in his own darkness again.
